summary: Plot a simulated image with **PyAutoGalaxy**, compare views of the dataset, and adjust the display so you can inspect its structure. This tutorial introduces the plotting tools used throughout the course.
title: Tutorial 0: Visualization

summary: Galaxies have a wide range of appearances: some are smooth and rounded, while others have discs, spiral arms or irregular structure. These visible features make up a galaxy’s **morphology**.

title: Tutorial 5: Summary

summary: In chapter 1, you adjusted a galaxy model by hand and inspected how well its image matched the data. Now we will ask a search to do this for us. Our aim is still to learn about the galaxy: its size, shape and concentration.
title: Tutorial 1: Non-linear Search

summary: A galaxy can contain a compact bulge and an extended disk. We now fit both, while learning how to run a search, manage its memory use and inspect its output. These practical skills let us assess a model as the fit progresses.
title: Tutorial 2: Practicalities

summary: The bulge and disk in tutorial 2 made our model more realistic, but also harder to fit. Their centres, shapes, brightnesses and sizes can trade off. A search can find a plausible galaxy without finding the best explanation available within the model.
title: Tutorial 3: Why Modeling Is Hard

summary: In tutorial 3, simplifying the bulge and disk geometry made the search easier but restricted the galaxies it could represent. Linear light profiles offer a different opportunity: keep the same profile shapes and solve their intensities directly, removing those dimensions from the non-linear search.
title: Tutorial 4: Linear Profiles

summary: So far we have changed the galaxy model and the search. Now consider the other side of the fit: the measurements we include and how they are compared with a prediction. The data, model and Analysis object have distinct jobs. This separation lets the same modelling tools work with different observations and likelihood functions.
title: Tutorial 5: Data and Likelihoods

summary: A neighbouring galaxy can complicate the fit to our target. We need to describe its light, but repeatedly searching all its parameters while refining the target can waste effort and introduce difficult degeneracies. Search chaining lets us fit different parts of the scene in stages.
title: Tutorial 6: Search Chaining

title: Tutorial 7: Summary

summary: Look at a resolved galaxy image. Its broad light distribution may follow a smooth bulge and disc, while smaller regions contain bright star-forming knots, off-centre clumps or irregular extensions. A model can capture the overall galaxy yet leave these features clearly visible in the residual image.

title: Tutorial 2: Bayesian Regularization

summary: A pixelization can describe a galaxy without assigning an analytic centre and shape to every visible feature. However, analytic profiles remain useful when we want to describe its smooth components. In this tutorial we combine an MGE with a pixelization and use search chaining to put the smooth light model in place first.
title: Tutorial 3: Model Fit

summary: Welcome to chapter 4 of **HowToGalaxy**, where we scale up galaxy modeling beyond a single galaxy.
title: Tutorial 1: Extra Galaxies

summary: In the previous tutorial, we learned how to deal with extra galaxies near the galaxy we care about — nuisance objects whose light contaminates the data but which are not themselves the subject of our study. We removed their emission from the analysis, or gave them a heavily restricted model, and the single galaxy we were studying remained the star of the show.
title: Tutorial 2: Multi-Galaxy Blends

summary: Throughout this chapter we have been scaling up: from a single galaxy with extra galaxies nearby, to blended multi-galaxy systems where every galaxy received its own free light model.
title: Tutorial 3: Cluster

summary: Return to this tutorial when a fit is too slow for your scientific needs. Faster likelihood calculations help, but a well-organised model and search often matter just as much. Hardware cannot make an inappropriate model fit.
title: Optional Tutorial: Need for Speed

summary: This is historical background, not part of the recommended HowToGalaxy learning path. Older versions of the PyAutoGalaxy / PyAutoLens workflow automatically narrowed priors between searches. That default behaviour has been disabled. New readers are discouraged from investing time in the old prior-passing recipes: learn the component-separation approach in chapter 2 tutorial 6 instead.
title: Optional Historical Tutorial: Prior Passing

summary: You can complete HowToGalaxy using Nautilus without studying search algorithms in detail. Return here if you want to understand the fast Prodigy stage of search chaining, or compare alternative approaches for your own work.
